## How this is estimated (and the research behind it)

Lean mass, not only muscle. The research measures lean mass: everything that is not fat. That is mostly muscle, but it also includes water and organs. This page says lean mass when it means the measured figure and muscle when it means the everyday idea.

The baseline share. Reviews of the trial data put lean mass at roughly 15 to 40 percent of the weight lost on a GLP-1 medication. [1] Within that spread, the medication matters. The estimator uses a baseline of about 33 percent for semaglutide and other GLP-1s, and about 26 percent for tirzepatide, the value measured in the DXA substudy of the SURMOUNT-1 trial. [1,4]

Why two scenarios. The share of loss that is muscle is not fixed. Without enough protein and without resistance training, the estimate sits at the high end of the published range, 40 percent for semaglutide. With both in place, it moves toward the low end. The size of that shift comes from a meta-analysis of older adults with obesity on caloric restriction, not GLP-1 users, where resistance training offset about 93.5 percent of the lean mass that dieting alone would cost. [2] Applying 93.5 percent to a GLP-1 baseline gives about 2 percent, which is an extrapolation, so the best case is shown as a range: that 2 percent floor up to 15 percent, the lowest lean-mass share reported in GLP-1 trials. [1] No trial has measured the 2 percent figure in people taking a GLP-1.

Your current-habits estimate. The headline range scales between those scenarios using your reported protein habit and resistance training. The two calculators on this site use the same shared numbers for the no-plan case. Protein and training both count, with training weighted as the primary driver because the offset in the research is a training effect. Protein enables it: benefit to fat-free mass leveled off near 1.6 g/kg of body weight, which is the target used here for the high-protein setting. [3]

Lean mass at risk. If you enter a goal weight, the tool multiplies each scenario's lean-mass share by the total weight you plan to lose, giving an approximate range of lean mass at stake. This is a projection from population ranges, not a prediction of your specific outcome.

## Honest limits

Every number here is an estimate assembled from group averages. The 15 to 40 percent range is wide because trials differ in population, dose, and how body composition was measured, and DXA itself carries error. The 93.5 percent offset is a single meta-analytic figure from people who were not taking a GLP-1, and it will not hold identically for every person or program. Your genetics, training quality, sleep, and starting body composition all move the real result. Treat this as a framework for a conversation with your clinician, not a measurement, a prediction, or medical advice.

## Frequently asked

**Q:** How much of GLP-1 weight loss is muscle?

Reviews of the trial data put lean mass at roughly 15 to 40 percent of the weight lost on a GLP-1 medication (Neeland 2024). The DXA substudy of the SURMOUNT-1 tirzepatide trial measured lean mass at about 26 percent of total loss. The exact share depends on the medication, your protein intake, and whether you do resistance training.

**Q:** How does this estimator work?

It starts from a published baseline share of lean mass for your medication (about 33 percent for semaglutide and other GLP-1s, about 26 percent for tirzepatide from the SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy), then shifts the estimate toward the low or high end of the published range based on your protein habit and resistance training. The shift uses the finding that resistance training offset about 93.5 percent of the lean mass that dieting alone would cost (Sardeli 2018). It is an illustrative projection from population ranges, not a measurement of your body.

**Q:** Can I lower how much muscle I lose?

The evidence points to two levers. Eat enough protein, around 1.6 g/kg of body weight or more, which is where benefit to fat-free mass leveled off in the research (Morton 2018). And do resistance training, which in a meta-analysis offset about 93.5 percent of the lean mass that caloric restriction alone would cost (Sardeli 2018). Together they move the estimate toward the low end of the range.

Two endings from the same start. Run the calculator above to see which muscle line your plan follows.

## How this is calculated (and the research behind it)

The anchor is trial-measured. In the STEP 1 trial extension, people who stopped semaglutide regained about two-thirds of their lost weight within twelve months: mean net weight loss fell from 17.3 percent to 5.6 percent. [1] That two-thirds figure is the red line, and it is what the best available trial shows for a full stop. Most people face this transition, since roughly 65 percent discontinue within a year. [2]

The taper and muscle lines are modeled, not measured. No trial isolates a taper schedule or a muscle-preservation protocol against regain, so the calculator projects a gradual taper and preserved muscle as reducing regain relative to a cold stop. That direction is well supported in principle, a slower return of appetite, continued treatment, and more metabolically active muscle all blunt rebound, but the exact size of the effect is an estimate. Treat the green line as a direction you can influence, not a promise.

Why muscle changes the picture. Reviews of GLP-1 body-composition data place lean mass at roughly 15 to 40 percent of total weight lost, [3] and resistance training has been shown to offset most diet-induced lean loss. [5] The regain risk is not only how many pounds return but their composition: regaining fat while muscle stays low trends toward sarcopenic obesity. [4] Arriving at your exit with muscle intact is the variable you most control.

## The four phases, and where muscle decides the ending

The diagram above traces the journey in four phases. During active loss the medication suppresses appetite and weight falls fast, and this is when composition is set, because without countermeasures roughly 15 to 40 percent of what you lose can be lean mass. [3] The plateau is where weight settles. The off-ramp, whether a cold stop or a gradual taper, is where appetite returns: in the STEP 1 trial extension people regained about two-thirds of their lost weight within a year of stopping semaglutide, and since roughly 65 percent of users discontinue within twelve months, most people reach this phase. [1] [2] Maintenance is the ending, and it splits in two. If you preserved muscle on the way down, you arrive with more metabolically active tissue and more reserve. If you did not, weight can return as fat while muscle stays low, the pattern that trends toward sarcopenic obesity. [4] The muscle you build during the loss phase is the reserve you spend later.

## Honest limits

The two-thirds figure comes from one population (semaglutide, STEP 1) and your result may differ. The taper and muscle adjustments are illustrative projections, not trial outcomes, and the curve shape assumes regain is front-loaded and then plateaus. This is a planning tool to show the shape of the risk and the levers you hold, not a prediction of your body. Decisions about staying on, tapering, or stopping a GLP-1 belong to you and your prescriber.

If 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg is hard to reach, is the range a four-society GLP-1 advisory uses during active weight loss. The target is scaled to total body weight, so it can run high if you carry a lot of fat mass. People with kidney disease should ask a clinician before raising protein.

## Where your weight loss comes from

Total loss is similar either way. What changes is how much of it is muscle.

Total weight lost Lean mass lost, without enough protein + training (40% of loss) Lean mass lost, with enough protein + training (best case, shaded range, 2 to 15% of loss; extrapolated from non-GLP-1 trials)

## Small-appetite meal plan

Your protein target split across the day, so no single meal has to be large.

Meal Time Protein

Tactics for low-appetite days

- Eat protein first, before other foods on the plate, so it lands even when you fill up fast.

- Use a liquid protein source (a shake, Greek yogurt, or milk) on nausea or low-appetite days, when solids feel like too much.

- Front-load protein earlier in the day, when appetite is usually highest.

- Time your largest protein meal away from the peak side-effect window after a dose.

## How this is calculated (and the research behind it)

Resting metabolism (BMR). The calculator uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, the predictive equation validated as most accurate for healthy adults. [1] For women it is 10 × weight(kg) + 6.25 × height(cm) − 5 × age − 161; for men the last term is + 5.

Total burn (TDEE). BMR is multiplied by a physical-activity factor (1.2 sedentary to 1.9 very active), the standard way to scale resting metabolism to real-world expenditure. [2] Your calorie target is TDEE minus the deficit implied by your chosen pace.

Weight-loss trajectory. The pace-to-deficit conversion uses the classic estimate that about 7,700 kcal equals one kilogram of body weight (3,500 kcal per pound). [3] This is a first approximation. Real loss slows over time as metabolism adapts, so a dynamic model predicts less than a straight line at the far end. [4] Treat the timeline as a planning estimate, not a promise.

Protein target. The 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg range comes from lean-mass research, where benefit to fat-free mass leveled off near 1.6 g/kg. [5] A GLP-1 advisory from four medical societies uses a lower range, 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg, which the calculator shows beside it. People with kidney disease should ask a clinician before raising protein. The target is split across your chosen number of meals because distribution matters more than any single dose. [6]

Meal timing on a small appetite. The same distribution logic is why the meal planner lets you spread the target across three to five meals: dividing protein into moderate servings through the day supports muscle better than concentrating it in one or two large meals, which is hard to eat anyway when a GLP-1 has cut your hunger. [6] On low-appetite days, eat protein first, front-load it earlier when hunger is highest, use liquid sources like a shake or Greek yogurt, and keep the biggest meal away from the peak side-effect window after a dose.

The two muscle lines. Reviews of the trial data put lean mass at roughly 15 to 40 percent of the weight lost on a GLP-1. [7] The dashed red line models the high end, 40 percent, that occurs without countermeasures. The green band models the outcome with adequate protein and resistance training. Its lower edge, about 2 percent, applies the finding that resistance training offset about 93.5 percent of the lean mass that caloric restriction alone would cost [8]; that result comes from older adults with obesity who were not taking a GLP-1, so it is an extrapolation. Its upper edge, 15 percent, is the lowest lean-mass share reported in GLP-1 trials. The muscle-loss calculator uses the same numbers. These are illustrative projections from published ranges, not a measurement of your body.

## Honest limits

Every number here is an estimate. Predictive BMR equations carry error at the individual level, the 7,700 kcal rule overstates loss over months, and the muscle split is modeled from population ranges rather than a scan of you. A target scaled to total body weight is a starting point, not a prescription, and it can overestimate protein for people carrying more fat mass. Use this as a framework, and confirm the specifics with your clinician, especially the calorie floor while on a GLP-1.

## Frequently asked

**Q:** How many calories should I eat on a GLP-1?

There is no single right number. The calculator estimates your maintenance calories (TDEE) from your sex, age, height, weight and activity level, then subtracts the deficit that matches the pace you pick, using the classic estimate of 7,700 kcal per kilogram of body weight. Change the pace and the target moves. It is a planning estimate: confirm the calorie floor with your clinician while on a GLP-1.

**Q:** How does this calculator estimate my calories?

It uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation for basal metabolic rate (BMR), the most validated predictive equation for healthy adults, then multiplies by a physical-activity factor to estimate total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). Your calorie target is TDEE minus the deficit implied by your chosen pace of weight loss.

**Q:** How much protein does it recommend, and of what type?

It applies the 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg of body weight range that lean-mass research supports during weight loss, split across four meals. Hit it from complete, leucine-rich sources; collagen is low in leucine and does little for muscle despite the label.

**Q:** Does the calculator work for women?

Yes. Choose your sex first: the Mifflin-St Jeor equation uses a different constant for women (minus 161) than for men (plus 5), so the calorie target differs. The protein target uses the same 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg range for everyone, scaled to body weight, and it can overestimate protein for people carrying more fat mass.

**Q:** How should I time meals when a GLP-1 has killed my appetite?

Spread your daily protein across three to five smaller meals rather than one or two large ones, because distributing protein through the day supports muscle better than loading it into a single meal. On a small appetite, eat protein first before other foods, front-load it earlier in the day when hunger is highest, lean on liquid sources like a shake or Greek yogurt on nausea days, and keep your largest meal away from the peak side-effect window after a dose. The calculator's meal planner shows the per-meal grams for the number of meals you choose.

**Q:** Why does the chart show a line and a band?

Total weight loss is driven by the calorie deficit and is similar either way. What changes is the composition. Without enough protein and resistance training, a large share of the weight lost is lean mass (reviews put it at 15 to 40 percent of GLP-1 weight loss). With adequate protein and resistance training, much of that is spared: a meta-analysis of older adults who were not on a GLP-1 found resistance training offset roughly 93.5 percent of the lean mass that dieting alone would cost, so the best case is shown as a range, not a single point. The red line and green band make that difference visible.

- Hall KD, Sacks G, Chandramohan D, et al. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. The Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826–837. doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60812-X

# GLP-1 split dose calculator

URL: https://getmuscleonglp.com/split-dose-calculator/

Free tool

Divide a weekly dose into smaller injections on an even schedule. This is arithmetic on the weekly dose your prescriber set. It does not suggest a dose, and splitting is not the schedule on the label.

Arithmetic only. This is not medical or dosing advice. It divides the weekly dose you enter and recommends no dose or schedule. A split schedule is not the one on the label. Confirm any change with your prescriber or pharmacist.

Example numbers: 1 mg a week split into 2 injections, semaglutide. Enter the weekly dose your prescriber set.

DayDoseSpacing

Splitting a weekly dose is not the labeled schedule. Ozempic and Zepbound are labeled for one injection a week, and we know of no published trial of splitting a weekly dose into smaller injections, so it has not been shown to be safer, better tolerated or more effective. This tool only does the division. Tell your prescriber before you change how you inject, and ask your pharmacist whether your pen or vial can deliver the smaller dose.

## How this is calculated

The dose. Each injection is the weekly total divided by the number of injections you pick, shown in milligrams to three decimals. Under the schedule the calculator adds the injections back up so you can see the weekly total is unchanged.

The days. Injections are spread as evenly as a seven-day week allows, counting from your first injection day. Two injections fall three and four days apart, three fall two, two and three days apart, and seven are daily.

What it leaves out. It works in milligrams only. It does not convert to syringe units or milliliters, because for a vial that depends on the concentration printed on the label and a mistake there changes the dose you inject. It knows nothing about your device, your dose history or your prescriber's instructions.

## What the labels say

The Ozempic label says to administer once weekly on the same day each week, at any time of day, with or without meals, and gives a half-life of approximately 1 week. [1] The Zepbound label says once weekly, at any time of day, tells patients to take a missed dose within 4 days (96 hours) or skip it, and gives a half-life of approximately 5 to 6 days. [2] The Zepbound label also lists single-dose pens and single-dose vials that each hold one labeled dose, and a multi-dose vial and KwikPen that hold four. [2] The missed-dose rules above belong to once-weekly dosing; they do not carry over to a split schedule.

## What is not known

Searches for a split dose calculator turn up many tools and many clinic blogs. What they do not turn up is trial data. The approved labels and the trials behind them used one injection a week, and we know of no published study of splitting a weekly dose into smaller injections. That does not make it dangerous, and it does not make it useful. It means nobody has measured it, so any claim that a split schedule is gentler or works better is a guess. If your prescriber recommended a split schedule, this page is a way to check the arithmetic. If you are considering one yourself, the conversation to have first is with them.

## Honest limits

The division is exact; everything around it is not. Rounding can leave the total a hair off, your device may not be able to deliver the smaller dose, and a schedule that is not on the label is one your prescriber and insurer may not expect. Treat the result as a way to talk to your prescriber, not a plan.

## Frequently asked

**Q:** How do I split a weekly Ozempic or GLP-1 dose?

Divide the weekly total your prescriber set by the number of injections, then space the injections as evenly as the week allows: two injections land on days 0 and 3 (for example Monday and Thursday). That is all this calculator does. Splitting is not the labeled schedule, so tell your prescriber before you change how you inject, and ask your pharmacist whether your pen or vial can deliver the smaller dose.

**Q:** Is it safe to split a weekly GLP-1 dose into two injections?

It has not been shown to be. The Ozempic and Zepbound labels specify one injection a week, and we know of no published trial of splitting a weekly dose into smaller injections, so there is no evidence that it is safer, better tolerated or more effective. If your prescriber chose a split schedule for you, follow their instructions. If you are thinking about it on your own, ask them first.

**Q:** Does splitting change the total weekly dose?

No. Two injections of half the weekly dose add up to the same total. The calculator shows that sum under the schedule, including when rounding to three decimals makes the total differ slightly.

**Q:** Does this convert milligrams to units or milliliters?

No, deliberately. It works in milligrams only. Converting to syringe units or milliliters for a vial depends on the concentration printed on that vial, and a mistake there changes the dose you inject. Ask your pharmacist or prescriber for that step.

**Q:** Does it work for tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound)?

The arithmetic is the same. The device is the catch: the Zepbound label lists single-dose pens and single-dose vials that each hold one labeled dose, so they cannot be divided, while its multi-dose vial and KwikPen hold four doses. Check your own product's label and ask your pharmacist.

## References

- Novo Nordisk. Ozempic (semaglutide) injection, prescribing information, section 2.1 (administration and missed dose) and clinical pharmacology (half-life). novo-pi.com/ozempic.pdf

- Eli Lilly and Company. Zepbound (tirzepatide) injection, prescribing information, section 2.3 (missed dose), dosage forms and strengths, and clinical pharmacology (half-life). pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf

# GLP-1 weight loss calculator

URL: https://getmuscleonglp.com/weight-loss-calculator/

Free tool

See what the average person lost on Wegovy, Ozempic, Zepbound or Mounjaro in the main trials, applied to your weight. Then see how much of that loss may be muscle, and what changes it.

Short answer. In the main trials, the average adult without diabetes lost 14.9% of body weight on Wegovy over 68 weeks and 15.0 to 20.9% on Zepbound or Mounjaro over 72 weeks. [1,3] People with type 2 diabetes lost less (7.0 to 9.6%). [2] Roughly 15 to 40% of that loss is lean mass, and protein plus resistance training push it toward the low end. [5]

A trial average, not a prediction. Individual results in every trial ranged widely around these averages. This gives no medical or dosing advice. Your prescriber sets your dose.

Weight at the trial's end if you matched its average (, source) Average loss applied to your weight What the placebo group lost with the same diet and activity advice

## How much of that could be muscle

Lean mass lost without enough protein or resistance training (high end of the published range) With 1.6 g/kg protein and 3+ training days a week (best-case range, partly extrapolated)

Run your own protein and training habits through the muscle loss calculator, or get your daily targets from the calorie and protein calculator.

## Every option side by side

Average percent weight loss in each trial's treatment arm. Sources: STEP 1, STEP 2, SURMOUNT-1, retatrutide phase 2. [1–4]

## How this calculator works

The calculator applies one number to your weight: the average percent change in the treatment arm of each drug's main trial. STEP 1 tested semaglutide 2.4 mg (Wegovy) in 1,961 adults without diabetes for 68 weeks. [1] STEP 2 tested semaglutide 1 mg and 2.4 mg in adults with type 2 diabetes for 68 weeks. [2] SURMOUNT-1 tested tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg (Zepbound, Mounjaro) in adults without diabetes for 72 weeks. [3] The retatrutide figure comes from a 48-week phase 2 trial of a drug that is not yet approved. [4]

The placebo figure matters as much as the drug figure. Every arm in these trials, placebo included, received diet and physical activity counseling. Therefore the gap between the two numbers is the drug's effect, and the placebo number is what the lifestyle advice alone produced.

The muscle estimate uses the same model as the site's other calculators. Reviews of the trial data put lean mass (everything that is not fat, mostly muscle plus water and organs) at 15 to 40% of GLP-1 weight loss. [5] The tirzepatide baseline is 26%, the share measured in the SURMOUNT-1 body-composition substudy. [5] The best case applies a resistance-training effect measured in older adults who were dieting without a GLP-1, so it is shown as a range rather than a single number. [6]

## Honest limits

Three limits apply. First, an average hides a wide spread: in STEP 1 about half of participants lost 15% or more, and some lost little. [1] Second, the trials ran 48 to 72 weeks, so the figures say nothing about year three or what happens after stopping (most people regain about two thirds of the loss within a year of stopping semaglutide). [7] Third, trial participants had close follow-up and counseling that everyday care may not match. Use this as a starting point for a conversation with your prescriber, not as a target.

## Frequently asked

**Q:** How much weight do people lose on Wegovy?

In STEP 1, adults without diabetes on semaglutide 2.4 mg lost an average of 14.9% of body weight over 68 weeks, compared with 2.4% on placebo. About half lost 15% or more. People with type 2 diabetes lost less: 9.6% on the same dose in STEP 2.

**Q:** How much weight do people lose on Zepbound or Mounjaro?

Both are tirzepatide. In SURMOUNT-1, adults without diabetes lost an average of 15.0%, 19.5% and 20.9% of body weight over 72 weeks on the 5, 10 and 15 mg doses, compared with 3.1% on placebo.

**Q:** How much weight do people lose on Ozempic?

Ozempic is semaglutide at diabetes doses up to 2 mg. The closest trial figure is the 1 mg arm of STEP 2, in adults with type 2 diabetes, who lost an average of 7.0% over 68 weeks versus 3.4% on placebo.

**Q:** How much of GLP-1 weight loss is muscle?

Reviews of the trial data put lean mass at roughly 15 to 40% of the weight lost. Protein of about 1.6 g/kg a day and regular resistance training are the two levers with evidence for moving it toward the low end. The full answer is here.
